comparator.name: Molecular and Biophysical Life Sciences
comparator.sourceNotes: The current official student curriculum states a complete 180-EC structure: 75 EC of mandatory foundation courses, a 15-EC bachelor research project, 45 EC of major-bound electives and 45 EC of free elective space. The programme page names the ten 7.5-EC mandatory courses. Students choose six major-bound electives, at least four at level 3, using four advisory profiles. The generic normalized target names no profile. Genes to Organisms is selected by official order, independently of UCR fit, and reconstructed with two level-2 and four level-3 courses marked for that profile in the official 2026-2027 overview. The free-elective space remains open.

comparatorRouteSelection.basis: The generic target does not name one of the four advisory elective profiles, and none is formally broader than the others. The current curriculum lists Genes to Organisms first, so it is selected by official order before UCR course selection. Six linked electives are instantiated while the separate 45-EC free-elective space remains open.

alternativeSelection.assessment: The broad closest match substantively covers the Genes to Organisms and Molecules & Cells directions. Molecules & Medicine and Biophysics & Modeling each generate a coherent, feasible and materially distinct UCR route. Their schedules differ pairwise by four to ten courses and pass all hard constraints, so the maximum of three alternatives is reached.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both establish foundations in cells, biomolecules, DNA and essential biological processes.
Both study proteins, nucleic acids, metabolism and the chemistry of biological processes.
Both connect genetic regulation and molecular change with development and disease; UCR is broader pathology and genetics.
Both connect molecular and cellular foundations to organismal and physiological function; UCR is human-centred.
Both study neural systems, biological mechanisms and behaviour; UCR provides an introductory rather than advanced molecular treatment.
Both examine immune mechanisms and interactions with pathogenic microorganisms.
Both examine molecular and cellular mechanisms whose disruption affects development and disease; UCR is broader disease mechanisms.
Both examine drug molecules, targets, action and disposition; UCR is pharmacology rather than organic synthesis.
Both develop practical molecular-biology and biochemical laboratory skills.
Both develop statistics and experimental analysis; Utrecht additionally integrates Python and academic writing.
The advanced research seminar develops research design and analysis, but does not reproduce Utrecht’s compulsory 15-EC laboratory thesis.
Both develop mathematics for quantitative life science; UCR does not combine this with programming in the same course.
Both apply contemporary quantitative technologies to biological or health problems; UCR contributes machine learning rather than biotechnology.
UCR has no scheduled course with the dedicated physical-chemistry and spectroscopy scope of this foundation.
UCR has quantitative and biological foundations but no dedicated biological-physics course matching this component.
UCR lacks a dedicated structural-biology and biophysical-methods course with microscopy and spectroscopy practice.
No single selected UCR course reproduces this integrated molecular-to-tissue component.
The 45-EC Utrecht free-elective space remains genuinely open and is not assigned invented UCR counterparts.

comparator.note: Genuine free elective space; no courses are invented for UCR convenience.

notes.text: Both programmes support substantial molecular, cellular, biomedical, quantitative and laboratory study. Utrecht additionally requires physical chemistry, biological physics, structural-biology methods, six major-bound electives and a 15-EC laboratory thesis. UCR can combine life science, biomedicine, data science and mathematics, but does not reproduce that full specialist chemistry/biophysics sequence or compulsory laboratory capstone.
